chapter_theme: Poems 361 to 380 move from death to the bard's reward. 361 to 367 are kaanchi counsel on impermanence: kings more than the sand have gone to the burning ground, so give, feast and act now (361 to 364, 366), or, in 365, the Earth herself weeps at being held by king after king. 368 to 373 are களவழி poems in which a drummer sings a king's battle as ploughing, sowing and threshing and asks for elephants as his share; 374 to 380 are kinai-drummers' praises of the givers Ay, Nalliyathan, Perunarkilli, Ilanchetchenni and the lord of Nanjil.

361.reading: The poet tells Death, who roars like thunder before the rains and is never sated with lives, that this king does not fear its coming: he has poured gifts with water for learned sacrificing brahmins, given like a mother to many, given elephants to those who sing him and chariots to those who come to his feet, drunk the toddy his women held to his lips like nectar, and needs no one to tell him that the world does not last, for he learned it long ago.
361.nuance: The poem is addressed to Death, not to the king, and turns the kaanchi lesson round: the counsel that the world is unstable is declared unnecessary, because a life of giving and enjoying has already answered it. The colophon has no thinai, thurai or poet.

thinai_evidence.note: impermanence is the theme, set against a life of giving

362.reading: A king with a gem necklace like the sun and moon on his chest, a drum fed with offerings in his camp and an army dreadful as a demon, mighty as Death, having cleared his confusion, pours gift-water wide as the sea, gives land, rice and splendid jewels, and then, while his kin go home from the burning ground of small white bones, where crows and owls call even by day, saying 'he is no more', goes on with his body to the land of the high ones.
362.nuance: Lines 8 to 10 contrast what a brahmin's four Vedas aim at with aram and with substance (பொருள்); their syntax is hard and the reading here is tentative. The closing image, going to the high world with the body, makes the gifts the king's last act rather than his reward, and the burning ground is drawn with the same small-white-bone detail the kaanchi poems share.

thinai_evidence.note: a king's last giving before death, with the burning ground described

comparisons.tenor: the gift-water poured from his hand

363.reading: The kings who ruled the sea-girt earth alone, sharing it with none, are more than the sand the waves heap up, and all went to the burning ground and died while others took their lands; so listen: no life stays with the body for ever and death is no illusion; before the bitter day when, in the burning ground of cactus, you eat with the earth for your plate the saltless boiled rice that a man of low birth hands over without looking back, do the work you intended, renouncing the whole sea-bounded world.
363.nuance: The humiliation is precise: the funeral offering is boiled without salt, handed over by an outcaste who does not turn to look, and eaten off the ground. The king who held the world 'with no share to others' ends taking food from the lowest. What the deed to be done is (giving, or renunciation) is left open by செய்ந்நீ முன்னிய வினையே.

thinai_evidence.note: impermanence of kings argued to move a king to act

comparisons.tenor: the number of kings who have died

364.reading: Let the bard-woman wear the unfading gold garland and the bard the gold lotus that blooms in no pool; let us roast the black ram on the red fire, turn the tongue over the spiced fat chunks in a toddy-reddened mouth, eat, devour and give to those who ask, and rejoice, warrior; for it will be hard, great one, when we have reached the great burning ground of urns, where the owl hoots suddenly from the hollow of an old tree with many roots split into the earth.
364.nuance: Kaanchi here means feasting, not renouncing: the same knowledge of death that makes 363 urge the king to give up the world makes this poet urge him to eat, drink and give now. The poet's name, கூகைக் கோரியார், is taken from the owl of line 12.

thinai_evidence.note: enjoy and give before the burning ground

365.reading: The wise say there is also a kaanchi in which the Earth, with the clouded sky for her face and the two moving lights for her eyes, wept: 'The ancestors who rolled the golden wheel of diamond hub and gem spokes before every battle and found no equal have gone, yet I do not go, and many still claim to be over me like a woman whose beauty is bought; I do not wish to live.'
365.nuance: The kaanchi is told from the side of the land, not the king: kings pass while the Earth stays, and her lament is not for their deaths but for being possessed by one after another, which she likens to a courtesan's lot. The poem presents itself as a report of a known kaanchi (உண்டென உரைப்பரால்), a poem about a genre.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem names its own kind as kaanchi: the earth's lament over passing kings

comparisons.tenor: the Earth claimed by many kings

366.reading: Even the great ones who ruled alone, whose drum roared like snake-striking thunder with one command through the land, set up their fame and died; so, son of the wise one, lord of warriors, hear me: [the text is broken here] use the day for effort and the night for weighing what is to come, drink sweet toddy in fine vessels with red-eyed women like a great ox released from the plough, give food and rice without stint, fell bulls and share the roast in every grove on the sandy bank, for death is real and no illusion.
366.nuance: Four lines are broken (7, 12, 16, 21), so the order of counsel is partly lost. What remains balances work by day (ஞாயிற்று எல்லை ஆள்வினைக்கு உதவி) with feasting and giving, and ends on the same line as 363. The colophon's patron தருமபுத்திரன் answers the poem's address அறிவோன் மகனே.

thinai_evidence.note: kings' deaths used to counsel a living king

comparisons.tenor: the king at his ease after labour

367.reading: Avvaiyar tells three crowned kings seated together, fair as the three sacred fires of the twice-born: the lands you hold do not go with you but stay for others; so pour flowers and gold with water into brahmins' hands, drink the toddy women bring in gold cups, scatter jewels to suppliants and live the days allotted, since only the good done while living is a raft when you sink; and may your days outnumber the stars and the raindrops.
367.nuance: Blessing and warning are one poem: the kaanchi doctrine that possessions stay behind is the reason given for the court's pleasures and gifts, and the blessing that closes it counts days, not conquests. The kings are not named; the colophon gives no patron.

thinai_evidence.note: a blessing addressed to kings, with counsel inside it

comparisons.tenor: the round earth the kings hold
the good deed done while living

368.reading: A drummer tells the Chera that he came to scoop up elephants, but all fell to arrows like hills that stop the clouds; chariots, but they lie broken on the ground; horses, but they lie dead and wounded in the flood of blood like ships becalmed; so on this cruel field where beggars grieve with nothing to take, ploughman whose plough is the sword, all his singing was to ask for the gem necklace on the king's chest.
368.nuance: The poem praises by complaint: the king's battle was so destructive that there is no war booty left to give, so the bard asks for the necklace he wears. The request formula முகக்குவம் எனின் (if we would scoop) frames the whole poem, as 372 and 371 use முகவை.

thinai_evidence.note: the king's victory sung by a bard at the battlefield

comparisons.tenor: the dead horses sunk in blood

369.reading: The bard sings the Chera's battle as a season of rain and tillage: elephants for clouds, swords for lightning, the drum for thunder, horses for wind, arrows for rain; chariots plough the wet field from dawn, spears sow it, fallen heads are the green crop, corpses the stacked sheaves that the demon-woman holds, jackals and ghouls thresh and spirits guard the heap; and he asks the lord of this field for a gift of elephants, cows like the gold-peaked Himalaya and their calves.
369.nuance: This is the fullest form of the ploughing figure that 368 compresses into one epithet and 373's colophon names ஏர்க்கள உருவகம். The bard's request is placed exactly where a harvest's share would fall, after the threshing, so the allegory carries a claim: the drummer is owed a portion of this crop as a labourer is of grain.

thinai_evidence.note: the king's battle as harvest, with the bard's claim

370.reading: With his large family starved to eating fibre and bark, the drummer crossed the parched long road where the owl's call answers the kite's mate in the uzhinjil fork and the bamboo has dried, and came like a bird to a fruiting tree to the field where weapons rained down fruit, blood flooded the ground, corpses were reaped, heaped and threshed with elephants for oxen; praising the field, he asks for elephants with iron-capped tusks, while the demon-woman dances decked in entrails and vultures circle.
370.nuance: The bard's hunger and the field's plenty are set side by side: the starving family of the opening is fed, in the figure, by the harvest of corpses. The first line is lost, and the review notes the opening lines read differently in another edition.

thinai_evidence.note: the battlefield praised as a harvest by a bard seeking a gift

comparisons.tenor: the bard coming to the king

371.reading: Finding no patron in the wide world, sleeping hungry under trees, his hair dressed with alari flowers tied on fibre, carrying his drum-bag and a useless broken pot with no rice in it, the drummer crossed the hard way to the camp, remembering the fame of the king's bow-plough that heaps headless corpses and threshes them with the elephant for ox; beating his moon-like drum he has come for an elephant, while the demon-woman, tasting fat and garlanded with entrails, blesses the giver of such plenty to live longer than the stars.
371.nuance: The demon-woman's blessing (வாழியர் ... பல) is the bard's own blessing displaced: the creature fed by the battle thanks the king, and the drummer, fed by nothing yet, asks to be next. According to the review's line table our text begins at the poem's third line.

thinai_evidence.note: the king's battle as threshing, with the bard's request

comparisons.tenor: the gleam of the iron weapons
the years wished for the king

372.reading: The drummer says all his praise was to ask for the king's moon-bright necklace: the king performed a sacrifice in the battlefield, where swords flashed and arrows rained, with enemy heads for the hearth, vilva wood for fuel and a vanni ladle, the demon who never bore a child stirring the pot, the cook holding up the lump of flesh, and the blessing 'may the ghoul-water poured in hot mouths fill all the new guests of this wedding feast'.
372.nuance: The sacrifice is a full parody of a Vedic rite and of a wedding feast at once, with every ritual item replaced by a battle one. Mangudi Kizhar uses the same figure of a feast cooked on crowned heads in 26 for the same king; here it is the preface to a request.

thinai_evidence.note: the king's battle as a field-sacrifice, praised by a bard

373.reading: The poet hails the victorious Chola who defeated the Kongu people: drums roared like thunder, war elephants were clouds, chariots and horses rain; swords dripped blood as if wrung; women left their high-walled houses; enemy kings turned their backs; mansions fell in flames like hills struck by thunder; he made the courtyard of Vanji a threshing floor and threshed the fearless warriors there; others came to every king's field for elephants, and he too, beating his drum for love, has come to this lord of the fearful field.
373.nuance: Eight lines are broken (9, 13, 14, 18, 22, 23, 27, 32), so the sequence of siege, sack and request is only partly recoverable. The colophon's second thurai, ஏர்க்கள உருவகம், names the ploughing figure that 368 to 372 share.

thinai_evidence.note: a city taken, its sack sung as threshing, with the bard's request

374.reading: At dawn in the cold dew, his thin hair damp like the gold-lit forehead of a blackbuck, leaning on the hill by the jackfruit of the common ground, the drummer sang the kurinji melody so that the stags listened, in the land where tiger-toothed boys and deer-eyed women heap porcupine meat, ripe sandal and elephant tusks on tiger skins as tribute; and he asks the sun whether it too has the generosity of Ay Andiran, or whether it shines in the sky for nothing.
374.nuance: The standard praise likens a giver to the sun or rain; this poem turns the measure round and finds the sun wanting. The colophon's பூவைநிலை usually names comparison of a king to a god; here the comparison is put as a challenge to the sky.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron's giving by a challenge to the sun

375.reading: Lodging in a corner of a ruined common hall with leaning pillars, his drum bundled with palmyra fibre and strips, never entering the ploughmen's households and asking who will take on his wretched life of begging by turns, the drummer came to Ay of unfailing giving thinking of him alone, as great rain spreads over the sea; so may Ay live on earth as the poets' home, and in a world empty of him let there be no patrons, lest our people sing kings of meritless wealth who understand nothing.
375.nuance: The close is a curse on the alternative more than a blessing: if Ay goes, the poet would rather there were no patrons than have his people praise kings who, told great things, grasp not even small ones. Lines 17 and 18 can be read otherwise, and the reading of நிலவன்மாரோ புரவலர் is uncertain.

thinai_evidence.note: praise and blessing of a patron by a needy bard

comparisons.tenor: the bard coming to Ay alone

376.reading: Just after sunset the drummer, holding his drum with its torn straps, stood at the granary of the patron's rich house; as the moon rose and drove off the dark, the great one saw his strange gaunt shape and his cloth worn to holes, called him a pitiable guest, stopped his song, and that same night gave him toddy fierce as an angry snake and roast meat and cleared his hell-like want; since that day he has not thought of begging, and his little drum has never sounded at the gates of other givers.
376.nuance: The gift is praised by its consequence: one night's giving ended a career of asking. The patron interrupts the song before it is sung (நின்ற முரற்கை நீக்கி), so the giving is not a payment for praise.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard's report of a patron's gift

377.reading: In the dewy watches of the night, his hair wet, the drummer came to the palace where the king slept and sang 'may the gods guard him, may the righteous one live'; the king, whom men call the one comparison for others with none for himself, saw him and called the far-travelling drummer his patron, and gave him, as if in a dream but awake, gems from the hills, gold from the forests, pearls from the sea, fine cloth and pots of toddy; and the poet blesses the victorious lord of the sea-loud army to last long.
377.nuance: Lines 10 and 11 state a theory of praise inside a praise poem: the king is the standard others are compared to, and nothing is his standard. The king's calling the bard 'patron to us' (நீ புரவலை எமக்கு) inverts the roles of giver and receiver. Two lines are broken.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a king's giving to a drummer

378.reading: In the Chola's palace, with stucco terraces like the new moon and a long hall cool as a pool, the drummer sang the vanji theme and the king showered on him more precious jewels than were ever meant for such as he; his long-starved kin put finger rings on their ears and ear rings on their fingers, waist chains on their necks and neck chains on their waists, like the red-faced monkey clan that found the jewels Sita dropped when the demon carried her from Rama, and had unending laughter; after great suffering he has become head of a large clan.
378.nuance: The Ramayana is cited for comedy: the monkeys decking themselves with Sita's jewels are the bard's family who have never owned ornaments. It is one of the few Sangam references to the Rama story, and it presupposes that the jewel episode was well known to the audience.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a king through the bard's report of his gift

comparisons.tenor: the bard's kin wearing the jewels wrongly

379.reading: Let me have life in the shade of his feet and let him have my tongue's praise: hearing your drummer say 'we are drummers of Villiyathan, lord of Ilangai of rich paddy, where reapers whose sickles blunt whet them on the curved back of a mud tortoise taking it for a stone; our lord melts fragrant ghee and gives daily rice and knows how to end hunger', my longing did not abate, and leaving the sky-touching hills behind I came like a child to its mother to that rich town whose fragrant smoke veils the streets like rain-mist.
379.nuance: The poem is built on report: the patron's fame reaches the poet through another drummer's speech, which the poem quotes, so one bard's praise becomes another bard's road. The tortoise mistaken for a whetstone makes the land's fertility comic and exact. Line 8 is obscure and line 14 broken.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron by a bard who comes to him

comparisons.tenor: the bard coming to the patron
the fragrant smoke over the streets

380.reading: The lord of Nanjil of the sweet jackfruit, a strong warrior of the Pandya, who wears pearls of the southern sea and sandal of the northern hill, in whose land rain becomes pearl in the sea and fragrant wild flowers flourish, is far beyond thought to those who meet him in enmity and close as the palm to those who come in friendship; because he is such, though this land should fall into want, the loneliness of the poet's family is gone and it has blossomed.
380.nuance: Three lines are broken (3, 8, 13), and line 12 mentions a Kandan of the strong spear whose relation to the patron is lost. The colophon fields were filled from Duraisamy Pillai's edition.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a chief through what he has done for the bard's family

links.note: Naladiyar 5 says those who gave first escape the waste land through which Death drags its captives; 361 tells Death to its face that a king who has given to brahmins, bards and suppliants does not fear its coming.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar's promise that givers escape Death is a future reward, while the Purananuru poet shows the same claim as a present state, a king already fearless, so the Jain maxim restates as doctrine what the court poets had staged as a king's achieved confidence.

links.note: Naladiyar 21: even umbrella-kings on elephants were carried off and none is left; 363: kings who ruled the whole earth alone are more than the sand and went to the burning ground, so act now and renounce.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar's general observation about dead kings appears in the Purananuru as an argument put to one living king, with the outcaste's saltless rice as its sting, which shows the impermanence of kings was a counsel form before it became a moral commonplace.

links.note: 364 answers the nearness of the burning ground with feasting: roast ram, toddy, gifts, joy now. Naladiyar 16 says joy that does not last, like the lamb nibbling its garland at the place of slaughter, is not found among the wise. On the plain reading, the feast 364 urges is exactly the lamb's pleasure the Naladiyar condemns.
links.teaches: Both poems draw their conclusion from the same nearness of death, so the disagreement shows that impermanence by itself did not settle how to live: the Sangam kaanchi poet drew enjoyment and giving from it, the Jain poet withdrawal.

links.note: In 365 the Earth, personified as a woman, weeps at being claimed by king after king like a bought woman; in Kural 1040 the good woman called Land laughs at those who sit idle pleading poverty.
links.teaches: The personified Earth judges men in both, but the Purananuru's Earth grieves at being owned by a succession of kings while the Kural's mocks those who do not work her, so the same figure speaks for the land against its rulers in one and against its idle tenants in the other.

links.note: Both close on the same line, மடங்கல் உண்மை மாயமோ அன்றே; 363 draws from it that the king should renounce the whole sea-bounded world (முழுதுடன் துறந்தே), 366 that he should work by day, drink with women and give food and bulls. The tension holds if துறந்தே in 363 means giving up rule, not only giving away.
links.teaches: A single refrain on death's reality served kaanchi poets as a premise for opposite conclusions, renunciation in one and feasting and giving in the other, so the formula was shared stock and the counsel was the poet's own choice.

links.note: Naladiyar 120: nothing goes with a person but the deeds they did; 367: the lands do not go with their owners, only the good done in living is a raft when one sinks, so give to brahmins and suppliants and drink the toddy women bring.
links.teaches: Avvaiyar and the Naladiyar hold the same doctrine that only deeds accompany a person, but Avvaiyar counts the court's feasting alongside giving as the way to use the allotted days, so the doctrine did not by itself require the ascetic conclusion the Jain anthology draws.

links.note: 368 calls the Chera 'ploughman whose plough is the sword' (வாளேர் உழவ) in a single epithet; 369 works the whole figure out: clouds, lightning, thunder, wind, rain, plough, seed, crop, sheaves, threshing and guarded heap.
links.teaches: Read together, the epithet in 368 turns out to be the compressed form of the full rain-to-harvest allegory in 369, and in both the bard's request stands where the labourer's share of a harvest would, so the figure carries the bard's claim to payment.

links.note: Both by Oonpothi Pasungudaiyar for Ilanchetchenni: 370 opens on the poet's large kin (இரும்பே ரொக்கற்கு) starving on fibre and bark and asks for elephants on the battlefield; 378 shows his kin (இரும்பேர் ஒக்கல்), long in want, decking themselves wrongly with the jewels the king poured out.
links.teaches: The two poems are the before and after of one bard's family under one patron, and the comedy of 378's misplaced jewels depends on the hunger 370 describes, so the pair records the bard's rise from want to a family that does not know how to wear wealth.

links.note: 371 recalls the king's fame as 'ploughing with the bow' (வில்லேர் உழவின்) and sings his battle as threshing; Kural 872 says one may take on the enmity of bow-ploughmen (வில்லேர் உழவர்) but not of word-ploughmen.
links.teaches: The Kural's bow-ploughman is a set epithet from the களவழி poems, where the battle is literally worked through as tillage and threshing, so the couplet takes the bards' highest praise of a warrior king and ranks it below the work of words.

links.note: Both by Mangudi Kizhar for Nedunchezhiyan: in 26 the king cooks a battlefield sacrifice with crowned heads as the hearth and blood as the water; in 372 the same field-sacrifice, with enemy heads as hearth stones and a demon stirring, is recited by the drummer who then asks for the king's necklace.
links.teaches: The same poet used the battlefield sacrifice once as direct royal praise and once as the set-piece before a bard's request, which shows the gruesome image had become a repertoire piece a performer could reuse to earn a gift.

links.note: Both by Mudamosiyar for Ay Andiran: 129 says the elephants Ay gave to suppliants outnumber the stars; 374 asks the sun whether it has Ay's generosity or shines in the sky for nothing.
links.teaches: The same poet twice measures Ay against the sky and twice finds the sky short, first in number and then in giving, so the reversal of the usual comparison of king to sun was his deliberate manner of praise, not a single conceit.

links.note: Kural 1061: not begging, even from those who give gladly without hiding, is worth ten million times more; 376: after one night's gift the drummer has not thought of begging since, and his drum has not sounded at other givers' gates.
links.teaches: The Kural reaches not-begging by self-respect, while the Purananuru bard reaches it because one patron gave so fully that no further asking was needed, so the poem shows the ideal attained from the giver's side rather than the asker's.

links.note: 378 likens the bard's kin decked in misplaced jewels to the monkeys who wore the jewels Sita dropped when Ravana took her; Akananuru 70 likens the hushed town to the banyan at Kodi that Rama silenced for his secret counsel.
links.teaches: The two Sangam allusions to the Rama story both use a marginal episode, dropped jewels and a silenced tree, as a simile for a crowd, so the story was known in enough detail that poets could cite its by-ways without telling it.

links.note: Both by Purathinai Nannaganar for an Oymaan chief: in 376 a drummer, given one night's gift, never begs again; in 379 the poet sets out because he heard another drummer quote the patron's habit of daily rice and ghee.
links.teaches: Read together, the satisfied drummer of 376 is the kind of witness whose report sets the poet of 379 on the road, so the gift was also the patron's advertisement and bards recruited one another to his gate.

links.note: 380 calls the patron தீஞ்சுளைப் பலவின் நாஞ்சிற் பொருநன் and says his giving made the poet's family bloom though the land be in want; 140 calls him தடவுநிலைப் பலவின் நாஞ்சில் பொருநன், who answered a request for a little rice with an elephant.
links.teaches: The jackfruit epithet for the Nanjil lord recurs in two poets, and 140's anecdote of overgiving supplies the deed behind 380's general claim that his family no longer feels want, so the chief's fame rested on a story bards shared.

new_concepts.gloss: the gift a bard seeks from a patron, and the asking for it
new_concepts.label_source: the colophon thurai of 379 names it (பரிசில்); the poems' own word for the gift asked on the battlefield is முகவை (370, 371, 373)

new_concepts.gloss: the battlefield sung as a threshing floor: a bard praises a king's battle as ploughing and harvest and asks for a share
new_concepts.label_source: the colophon thurai மறக்களவழி (368 to 371, 373); 373 adds ஏர்க்கள உருவகம், and 372 has மறக்கள வேள்வி

source_issues: 361: the colophon has no thinai, thurai, poet or patron.
361 line 9: கொன்றுதன் kept; another edition reads கொன்றதன் (flagged). The review's line table says we lack a final line (site line 23).
363 line 9 and 366 line 22 are the same line (மடங்கல் உண்மை மாயமோ அன்றே); a shared kaanchi refrain, not a copying error.

366: lines 7, 12, 16 and 21 are broken; editions differ on lines 16 and 21 (one fills the lacuna and adds a line, with lines 16 to 19 in another order). The review lists 366 among poems whose line breaks differ.
370 line 1 is lost except its last syllable; the review says lines 1 and 2 read differently in another edition. 370 line 27 repeats 373 line 39, a closing formula of the களவழி poems.
370: the colophon patron reads செரப்பாழி இறிந்த, a misprint for எறிந்த (378's colophon has செரப்பாழி எறிந்த).
371: the review's line table says our text lacks the poem's first two lines (it starts at its third). Line 11 is broken. Line 21 களிற்றுக்கோட்ட டன்ன has a doubled ட (களிற்றுக்கோட்டன்ன).
372: the colophon thurai மறக்கள வேள்வி is normalised as மறக்களவேள்வி.

373: lines 9, 13, 14, 18, 22, 23, 27 and 32 are broken; lines 18 and 23 begin with a dead consonant (lost letters); the review lists 373 among poems with stray non-Tamil glyphs and lines 13, 18, 22 reading differently. Line 11 நெடுங்சுவர் is a misprint for நெடுஞ்சுவர்.
374 line 4 repeats 383 line 2, and line 6 repeats 397 line 10: formula lines of the kinai poems. The review says line 10 reads differently in another edition.
374 and 375: the poet is spelt உறையூர் ஏணிச்சேர் முடமோசியார் in 374 and உறையூர் ஏணிச்சேரி முடமோசியார் in 375.
377: lines 23 and 26 are broken; line 8 has a stray opening quotation mark; the review says the site lacks our line 22 and we lack two of its lines (line breaks differ).
